summary.text: 对 is the simplified form of 對. The older graph has a disputed interpretation as a hand, a possible tool, and earth, but its earliest meaning is unresolved. Early Western Zhou inscriptions use 對 in formulas with disputed force; later texts use it for “reply” or “answer.” Modern meanings include “correct,” “right,” “facing,” and “opposed.”

formation.text: Traditional 對 has competing analyses. One reads 又 as a hand, 丵 as a possible tool, and 土 as earth in a land-working scene. Another proposes that 丵 and 土 together serve as a sound element, but supplies no reading for 丵 to compare with 對. Neither analysis settles the graph’s earliest meaning.

components.text: In the proposed land-working interpretation of traditional 對, 又 depicts the hand. The modern 又 + 寸 analysis of 对 does not show that the older graph began as a pair of hands.

One analysis identifies 丵 as a digging tool; others identify a punitive instrument or toothed weapon. The object and its original name are uncertain. Another proposal treats 丵 with 土 as a sound element, but provides no reading for 丵 to test against 對.

sound_limitation.text: No reading for 丵 is supplied for comparison with 對, and the alleged implement’s name and pronunciation are unavailable. This limitation does not establish the proposed phonetic role.

components.text: In the proposed land-working scene for traditional 對, 土 depicts earth. Historical forms also show disagreement between 土 and 士, but no specific alteration event or secure sequence among these forms is established.

history.text: A modern redraw in oracle-script style shows branching upper strokes, hand-like strokes at lower left, and a long descending stroke on the right. It illustrates the proposed 丵, 又, and 土 analysis but does not establish that interpretation or a sequence of forms.

The received Shuowen account gives 𡭊 as the head form, analyzed as 丵, 口, and 寸, and records 對 as an alternative said to substitute 士 for 口. Other evidence reports 土 in ancient and clerical forms. No specific alteration event or secure ancestor-descendant sequence is established.
In the modern standard, 对 corresponds to traditional 對. The earlier history and adoption pathway of 对 are unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The earliest meaning of 對 is unresolved. Oracle-bone uses have been proposed as a sacrificial or place name, but no specific specimen, context, or meaning is established; land working is not a secure earliest sense.

The land-working interpretation competes with other identifications of 丵 and with a proposal that 丵 and 土 together serve as a phonetic element. No reading for 丵 is supplied to test that proposal against 對’s word reading.

Reuse of the whole graph for “reply” on the basis of sound is not verified: the alleged object’s name and pronunciation are unavailable. Reconstructions of 對 concern the word “respond,” not the alleged implement.

A hand 寸 holding a lit 业 candelabrum 羊
Origin unclear. Appears to be a hand using some sort of tool, possibly a rake or a hoe.
譍無方也。从丵从口从寸。

In the oracle bone and bronze scripts, it was an ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 丵 (“tool for digging”) + 土 (“earth”) + 又 (“hand”). The original meaning of the character is unclear, but it may be “to develop (land)”. It was later borrowed for “to reply”. Compare 封, 邦.
In the seal script, 又 has become the related 寸. Shuowen has two seal script forms for this character: 𡭊 (main form) and 對 (alternative form). The main form, which has a 口 (“mouth”), was probably created to specialize the character to signify “to reply”, but this form was not inherited in later scripts. Shuowen interprets the latter form (shown above) as a form that Emperor Wen of Han created by replacing 口 with 士 (“soldier; warrior”) because many of the replies were untruthful (just lip service), but it is more likely that 士 is a corruption of 土.
Exoactive of 答 (OC *tkuːb, “to reply; to answer”) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 as transcribed by Shuowen.org; commentary by 段玉裁
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry gives the head form 𡭊 as “respond without fixed form,” analyzed as 丵 + 口 + 寸. It records 對 as an alternative form, said to replace 口 with 士 under Emperor Wen. Duan Yucai explains the response metaphor through a bell answering knocks of different force, and reads 寸 as measure or rule. These are historical claims by Xu Shen and Duan, not independent confirmation of the graph’s earlier structure. The same page’s note says editions/readings differ between 士 and 土.
evidence.title: 說文解字「對」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The database reports oracle-bone forms analyzed as 又 + 丵 + 土, and bronze forms with an added 丰-like element. It presents a proposed interpretation: 丵 as a digging implement, with the graph depicting a hand using a tool to work land; the bronze form is associated with planting or marking boundaries. It reports oracle-bone instances as possibly a sacrificial or place name, while early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use 對 in response/acknowledgment formulas, including 大盂鼎 “用對王休.” These are the database’s scholarly synthesis, not a visually inspected glyph analysis in this research.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 對

evidence.text: The museum identifies 大盂鼎 as an early Western Zhou vessel and dates it, under its cited chronology, to King Kang’s twenty-third year (998 BCE). Its inscription ends “盂用對王休，用作祖南公寶鼎.” The museum describes the text as a royal investiture and rewards, followed by Yu’s commemorative vessel. This securely dates the written formula but does not by itself settle whether 對 here means answer, repay, acknowledge, or another related act.
evidence.title: 大盂鼎

evidence.source: 鄭州大學文學院 article on Western Zhou bronze inscriptions
evidence.text: The article reports that 對揚 and related formulas occur hundreds of times in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, often in the transition from recorded royal gifts or commands to the reason for making and inscribing the vessel. It summarizes traditional explanations as a recipient’s response and praise or thanks, and also describes a dissenting ritual interpretation. Thus bronze “對” evidence is early and abundant, but its precise pragmatic force is disputed.
evidence.title: 西周铜器铭文文学功能观初论

evidence.text: This article lists multiple early and middle Western Zhou vessel examples containing 對揚 and related phrases, with vessel catalogue references and proposed readings as expressions of thanks or acknowledgment. It supports early bronze use of 對 in the formula, but does not establish a land-working-to-reply semantic chain.
evidence.title: 金文“休”字意义补说

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The official variant dictionary notes the Shuowen variant explanation but observes that ancient writing and clerical script often show 土, and that Duan Yucai acknowledged editions and rhyme books read 土. It says the later standard form has the structure now written 對. Its sense citations include the Zhou poem 桑柔, “聽言則對,” and a 春秋傳 episode, “公問之。對曰…”. It treats response as the first listed sense and gives later extensions separately, without claiming a dated chain for every extension.
evidence.title: [A01066] 對 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 古文島 transcription of 左傳·隱公元年
evidence.text: The text gives “公問之。對曰：小人有母……” and identifies 隱公元年 as 722 BCE. This is a dated narrative setting in the transmitted text, not direct evidence that the extant written form of the graph was inscribed in 722 BCE; it documents the lexical use of 對 as an answer in the received text.
evidence.title: 左传·隐公·隐公元年

evidence.text: The table explicitly lists 对〔對〕 among simplified-character correspondences. This supports the modern standard relation between the simplified graph 对 and traditional 對; it does not establish the formation history of either ancient graph.
evidence.title: 简化字总表（1986年版）

evidence.text: The entry identifies 对 as the simplified form of 對 and gives a modern component description 又 + 寸. That description applies to the simplified written shape as a modern component analysis; it is not evidence that the ancient 對 graph was formed from a pair of hands or that 对 independently originated with that meaning.
evidence.title: 对 duì - 汉典

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction database v1.1
evidence.field: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese pronunciation entry for 對
evidence.text: The database gives modern Beijing pinyin duì, Middle Chinese twojH, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[t]ˤ[u]p-s for 對, glossed “respond.” Its introduction defines square brackets as uncertainty about a segment’s identity, here the stop coda as potentially *-t or *-p. This entry is phonological reconstruction for 對’s word, not a reconstruction of any depicted tool name.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.source: Zhengzhang Shangfang system as reported in the Chinese Wiktionary entry; corroborated as a separate system by the dossier’s Zhengzhang record
evidence.text: The entry reports Zhengzhang (2003) *tuːbs for 對, contrasted with Baxter–Sagart *[t]ˤ[u]p-s. These are system-specific reconstructions of the character’s word; neither establishes the unrecoverable original pronunciation of an alleged depicted implement.
evidence.title: 對 - 维基词典

evidence.source: Cambridge University Press article, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
evidence.text: The article reconstructs 對 ‘respond’ as Old Chinese *tˤup-s and Middle Chinese twojH, relating it probably to synonymous 答 ‘answer’ reconstructed *tˤup. This is a proposed word-level etymological relation and sound-history analysis. It does not identify the original referent/name of the components in the old 對 graph and does not, by itself, prove whole-graph borrowing from a land-working word.
evidence.title: Bai and Old Western Chinese

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: Its analysis treats 丵 as the depicted digging tool, 土 as worked soil, and 又 as the hand in the proposed land-working interpretation. It does not analyze any component as a phonetic. The same database says 丵 has competing identifications in scholarship, including derivation from 䇂 (a punitive instrument) and an interpretation as a toothed ancient weapon; these alternatives leave the precise original depicted object uncertain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 對

evidence.source: Duan Yucai commentary quoted in Shuowen.org; Taiwan Ministry of Education variant dictionary
evidence.field: 士 versus 土 graphic relationship
evidence.text: Shuowen gives the alternative form with 士 and explains it as Emperor Wen’s replacement for 口. Duan’s note says editions and rhyme books show 土 and leaves the reading unresolved; the Taiwan MOE dictionary says ancient and clerical forms often have 土 and that this is the later conventional form. Consequently the graphic evidence supports 土 as a recurrent historical shape and makes the received moralizing account questionable, but the cited pages do not document a specific corruption event or establish a dated ancestor-descendant relation for every form.
evidence.title: [A01066] 對 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: Chinese phonological readings listed with graph history
evidence.text: For the character 對, the database reports Mandarin duì, Cantonese deoi3, Middle Chinese fanqie 都隊切 with a departing tone in the 灰/隊 rhyme, and Tang-period reconstruction *duə̀i. These are readings of 對, not of a separate sound component, since no phonetic component is proposed in this analysis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 對

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義源流通解；甲骨、金文字例
evidence.text: The entry reports oracle-bone 對 forms analyzed as 又 + 丵 + 土, and says bronze forms add a 丰-like element below 丵. It presents a land-working and boundary-marking interpretation as a scholarly proposal, followed by borrowing for response/answer. It reports oracle-bone uses as possibly a sacrificial or place name, and cites Western Zhou bronze formulas including 大盂鼎 “用對王休.” The source also records competing views of 丵: a digging tool, an element derived from 䇂, or a toothed ancient weapon. This is the database’s synthesis, not independent confirmation of the proposed semantic chain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「對」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry proposes that the upper 丵 and lower 土 may function together as a phonetic element, citing 陳秉新, while treating 又 as the hand in its land-working analysis. This differs from treating the entire graph as a purely semantic compound. The same entry gives Mandarin duì and Guangyun 都隊切, with departing tone and 灰/隊 rhyme classification. It does not provide a matching reconstruction for 丵 as a component, so the proposed component-level phonetic analysis cannot be tested here against 對 in one reconstruction system.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「對」

This is a proposed word-level etymological relation and sound-history analysis. It does not identify the original referent/name of the components in the old 對 graph and does not, by itself, prove whole-graph borrowing from a land-working word.
evidence.title: Bai and Old Western Chinese

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: Its analysis treats 丵 as the depicted digging tool, 土 as worked soil, and 又 as the hand in the proposed land-working interpretation. It does not analyze any component as a phonetic. The same database says 丵 has competing identifications in scholarship, including derivation from 䇂 (a punitive instrument) and an interpretation as a toothed ancient weapon; these alternatives leave the precise original depicted object uncertain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 對

evidence.source: Duan Yucai commentary quoted in Shuowen.org; Taiwan Ministry of Education variant dictionary
evidence.field: 士 versus 土 graphic relationship
evidence.text: Shuowen gives the alternative form with 士 and explains it as Emperor Wen’s replacement for 口. Duan’s note says editions and rhyme books show 土 and leaves the reading unresolved; the Taiwan MOE dictionary says ancient and clerical forms often have 土 and that this is the later conventional form. Consequently the graphic evidence supports 土 as a recurrent historical shape and makes the received moralizing account questionable, but the cited pages do not document a specific corruption event or establish a dated ancestor-descendant relation for every form.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: Chinese phonological readings listed with graph history
evidence.text: For the character 對, the database reports Mandarin duì, Cantonese deoi3, Middle Chinese fanqie 都隊切 with a departing tone in the 灰/隊 rhyme, and Tang-period reconstruction *duə̀i. These are readings of 對, not of a separate sound component, since no phonetic component is proposed in this analysis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 對

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義源流通解；甲骨、金文字例
evidence.text: The entry reports oracle-bone 對 forms analyzed as 又 + 丵 + 土, and says bronze forms add a 丰-like element below 丵. It presents a land-working and boundary-marking interpretation as a scholarly proposal, followed by borrowing for response/answer. It reports oracle-bone uses as possibly a sacrificial or place name, and cites Western Zhou bronze formulas including 大盂鼎 “用對王休.” The source also records competing views of 丵: a digging tool, an element derived from 䇂, or a toothed ancient weapon. This is the database’s synthesis, not independent confirmation of the proposed semantic chain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「對」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry proposes that the upper 丵 and lower 土 may function together as a phonetic element, citing 陳秉新, while treating 又 as the hand in its land-working analysis. This differs from treating the entire graph as a purely semantic compound. The same entry gives Mandarin duì and Guangyun 都隊切, with departing tone and 灰/隊 rhyme classification. It does not provide a matching reconstruction for 丵 as a component, so the proposed component-level phonetic analysis cannot be tested here against 對 in one reconstruction system.

evidence.text: The file page identifies this as a modern SVG depiction of 對 in oracle-script style, states that it is based on Xiaoxuetang, and lists component tags 丵, 土, 又. Its reuse notice describes the representation as public domain and says attribution is appreciated but not required. This is a modern redraw, not a photograph or facsimile of an inscribed artifact; the file page does not give a specific inscription or date for the depicted form.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The oracle-bone forms reported in the CUHK database are dated by script period, but this research did not open individual rubbing records or inspect glyph images; it therefore does not verify each form’s reading or inscriptional context independently.

The cited database reports oracle-bone uses as a possible sacrificial or place name, but no specific item, date, context, or sense evidence was inspected. The earliest semantic value of the graph remains unresolved.

The proposed land-working and boundary-marking interpretation is not independently established here. The semantic transitions from land working/boundary marker to the recorded bronze acknowledgment and reply senses are not documented as a continuous dated chain.
The meaning of 對 in early “用對王休” and “對揚王休” bronze formulas is debated; response, acknowledgment/repayment, praise, and ritual-action analyses cannot be collapsed into one certain gloss.

The asserted whole-graph loan from a land/boundary graph for “reply” remains unproven in the sources inspected. The Cambridge paper discusses a probable word-level relation between 對 ‘respond’ and 答 ‘answer’, not an independently recovered object name or the graphic borrowing mechanism.

No phonetic component is identified in the source-supported accounts, so there is no proposed sound component for which a component-versus-character pronunciation comparison can be made. The alleged tool/object represented by 丵 has competing interpretations and its name/pronunciation is not recoverable from the inspected evidence.

The Shuowen Emperor Wen explanation is a historical account, not proof of the alternative graph’s creation. Sources support recurrent 土 forms and disagreement over 士/Tu readings, but not a specific corruption mechanism or a secure chronological ancestry classification among all variant shapes.

The modern standard relation 对〔對〕 is verified in the 1986 table, but the exact earlier history of the simplified form 对, including the earliest dated appearance and adoption pathway, was not established.

Although dictionaries quote the Zhou poem 桑柔 for “answer/reply,” no independent manuscript dating or early inscriptional attestation for that particular line was obtained here; literary use is reported as a transmitted textual witness, not a directly dated graph specimen.

The repository’s E1 claim “a pair of hands 又 寸” describes simplified 对 and should not be transferred to traditional 對’s oracle/bronze structure. E5’s “lit candelabrum” component reading was not supported by the sources inspected.
The image candidate is a modern redraw in oracle-script style, not an artifact photograph; its page does not identify a specific bone inscription or date for this particular glyph.
The Xiaoxuetang record page returned an internal error when opened, so no exact database image or label was selected.

The queried sources disagree about whether 丵 is a digging implement, derives from a punitive instrument, or represents a toothed weapon. The depicted object and its original name and pronunciation remain unestablished.

CUHK’s suggested land-working/boundary sense and subsequent borrowing for response are hypotheses; the inspected page does not establish a dated continuous semantic chain. Early bronze formula semantics are not settled by this character entry alone.

CUHK reports an alternative proposal that 丵 + 土 may form a phonetic element, but no component reconstruction was obtained here to compare with the character’s readings. The entry’s Mandarin and Guangyun information concerns 對 itself.
No candidate image was visually inspected during this research stage; the harness’s later pixel inspection is needed to assess whether the proposed redraw accurately illustrates the described form.

items.period: Labeled oracle-script style; the file page gives no specific inscription date
items.tradition: Oracle-script style; modern vector redraw based on Xiaoxuetang
items.caption: A modern redraw of 對 in an oracle-script style. The form has a branching upper element, a hand-like lower-left stroke, and a long descending stroke on the right. One analysis reads it as 又, 丵, and 土 and proposes a land-working image, though both the object represented by 丵 and the graph’s earliest sense remain uncertain.
items.alt: Black oracle-script-style form on white: branching strokes at the top, a hand-like shape at lower left, and a long curved stroke descending at right.
items.selection_reason: This specifically identified 對 redraw illustrates the reported early form and its proposed component analysis. Its visible structure suits that discussion, while the interpretation remains a scholarly proposal.
items.rights: Public domain dedication for the modern SVG representation, according to its Wikimedia Commons file page.

limitations.text: The image is a modern vector redraw, not an artifact photograph or a dated inscriptional specimen. The candidate’s specific date and context are unknown.
The proposed land-working interpretation is uncertain: 丵 has competing identifications, and the earliest sense of 對 and any continuous path to its later response use are not established.
